quote: I am not predicting that AI will fail to achieve super-human intelligence. Like many of my colleagues working in AI, I predict we are just 30 or 40 years away from this event. However, I am suggesting that there will not be the run away exponential growth predicted by some.
claim_summary: In his paper 'The Singularity May Never Be Near', Walsh predicts AI will reach super-human intelligence in 30 or 40 years, like many of his AI colleagues, while arguing against a runaway singularity.
definition_note: super-human intelligence reached without a runaway technological singularity
notes: computed: 2016 + 30 and 2016 + 40; basis: "I predict we are just 30 or 40 years away"; Paper "The Singularity May Never Be Near", arXiv 1602.06462 version 1, read in full in the ar5iv HTML copy; date is the arXiv submission date (abstract page: "Submitted on 20 Feb 2016"). He presented it at the AAAI-16 AI, Ethics and Safety workshop on 2016-02-13 (Future of Life Institute report, futureoflife.org, 2016-02-17). One row per capability (A15 ruling 13): this row is the super-human intelligence date; walsh-2016-01b is the runaway growth claim in the same passage. "this event" refers back to AI achieving super-human intelligence. The conclusion of the same paper repeats the position: "even without a technological singularity, we might still end up with machines that exhibit super-human levels of intelligence" (not a separate row; same occasion). Panel verification described the target as human-level; the words say super-human, so superintelligence.

quote: He argues that computers will reach and then quickly exceed the intelligence of humans, and that progress will “snowball” as computers redesign themselves and exploit their many technical advantages. The movie of Ray’s book is coming to a theatre near you soon. Fortunately, I do not share Ray’s concerns. There are several problems with his argument.
claim_summary: Writing after IBM's Watson won Jeopardy!, Walsh describes Kurzweil's singularity (computers exceeding human intelligence and snowballing as they redesign themselves) and says he does not share that view, giving reasons against it.
definition_note: Kurzweil's singularity: computers exceed human intelligence and progress snowballs as they redesign themselves
notes: basis: "I do not share Ray’s concerns"; His own article in The Conversation, "Have computers finally eclipsed their creators?", read in full at theconversation.com (fetched with curl); date from the page metadata and his author listing (2011-03-27). Ambiguous field: endorsement. "concerns" refers back to Kurzweil's argument for a snowballing singularity, and the next sentences argue against it ("no reason to suppose that there is much special in exceeding human intelligence"; physical limits such as the speed of light), so rejects; but "concerns" could also be read as rejecting only the worry, not the forecast. He does not reject that computers will exceed human intelligence. Target: the words describe computers that "redesign themselves" with progress that snowballs, which is the successive-rounds case, so si_sustained. Kurzweil's "around 40 years" is Kurzweil's date, not Walsh's, so no timeline. The same article opens by calling Watson "another step towards the ultimate goal of creating and perhaps exceeding human-level intelligence" (not coded separately).

quote: AI that might threaten our society’s future is likely still some way off. AI researchers have been predicting it will take another 30 or 40 years now for the last 30 or 40 years. And if you ask most of them today, they (as I) will still say it is likely to take another 30 or 40 years.
claim_summary: Responding to Hawking's warning about 'full artificial intelligence', Walsh says AI capable of threatening society is still some way off and that he, like most AI researchers, would say it is likely to take another 30 or 40 years.
timeline_text: likely still some way off ... likely to take another 30 or 40 years
definition_note: AI that might threaten society's future, in reply to Hawking's 'full artificial intelligence'; the next sentences speak of 'replicating the sort of intelligence that humans display'
notes: computed: 2015 + 30 and 2015 + 40; basis: "they (as I) will still say it is likely to take another 30 or 40 years"; The quote starts mid-sentence; the full sentence opens "My opinion (and one many of my colleagues share) is that". His own article in The Conversation, "Artificial Intelligence should benefit society, not create threats", read in full at theconversation.com (fetched with curl); date from his author listing (2015-01-15). Target judgment: "AI that might threaten our society’s future" answers Hawking's "full artificial intelligence", and the article goes on to say replicating human intelligence will need significant advances, so broad_competence. "likely" with "will still say" read as acceptance, as "still likely decades away" is in the codebook (marcus-2022-04). The threat is mentioned but no consequence is forecast, so consequence fields unspecified.

definition_note: 'true artificial intelligence' delivered as a phone assistant that understands spoken requests in all major languages
notes: His contribution to a group piece in The Conversation, "It’s Back to the Future Day today – so what are the next future predictions?", in which contributors imagined technology on 2045-10-21; read in full at theconversation.com (fetched with curl); date from his author listing (2015-10-20). Judgment call on whether it qualifies: it is a playful scenario written in the present tense, not a forecast he argues for, but it puts a year on "true artificial intelligence", so it is recorded and flagged rather than dropped. Ambiguous fields: endorsement (scenario writing, treated like a joke under the codebook: unexpressed) and target_capability (the words say "true artificial intelligence", but what is described is an assistant that understands requests, so conversation rather than broad_competence). Not a firm prediction; low confidence.

definition_note: human-like artificial intelligence: reproducing or exceeding the capabilities of the human brain
notes: basis: "It is 100% plausible that we’ll have human-like artificial intelligence"; The Conversation panel piece "Your questions answered on artificial intelligence", in which academics answered readers' questions; his answer to Q1 "How plausible is human-like artificial intelligence?", read in full at theconversation.com (fetched with curl); date from his author listing (2015-11-15). Elicitation interview: he is answering a posed question. The same piece has answers by Kevin Korb and Rob Sparrow, who are not on the panel (not recorded). "or exceeding its capabilities" also raises superintelligence as possible (kept in this row; the lead claim is human-like AI).

The concern raised instead, "incompetent machines", is coded other_concern with reliability.
